UNIT 11: COASTAL PROCESSES, LANDFORMS AND MANAGEMENT

KEY THEME
- The sea transforms the landscape through wave action in three main ways: erosion (wearing it away), transportation (moving its load along the coast) and deposition (dropping its load).
- Learning outcomes: name and explain coastal erosion, transportation and deposition; describe how coastal processes shape the Irish landscape by forming landforms; understand and discuss coastal management strategies in Ireland.

INTRODUCTION
- Coast: a narrow zone where the land and sea meet.
- The Irish landscape is constantly shaped by waves, which erode, transport and deposit coastal material.

THE POWER OF WAVES
- The power of the sea comes from the millions of waves that strike the coast every year.
- Waves are created far out at sea where wind blows over the water surface, creating friction and changes in pressure.
- Crest: the top of a wave (pulled up). Trough: the dip of a wave (pushed down).
- The water rolls in a circular orbit, which creates a wave as it travels along. In deep water, waves have an orbital shape.
- Diagram (Fig 11.1): close to the shore, friction with the rough seabed slows the base of the wave; waves become elliptical, rise in height and lean forward; the wave breaks and rushes towards the shore.

HOW A WAVE WORKS
- The size and energy of waves depend on three things: the strength of the wind; the length of time the wind has been blowing; the fetch.
- Fetch: the distance of ocean over which the wind blows and the waves build up.
- The west coast of Ireland has a huge fetch of thousands of kilometres across the Atlantic. This is why Lahinch, Co. Clare and Easkey, Co. Sligo are great for surfing.
- Geofact: it is 6,233.4 km from San Juan, Puerto Rico to Galway Bay; the prevailing winds and fetch in the west usually follow this route.
- The east coast has a smaller fetch, so Howth (Co. Dublin), Bettystown (Co. Meath) and Bray (Co. Wicklow) do not get big waves as often.
- As waves move from deep to shallow water they slow down, become steeper and move closer together (shorter wavelength). The circular orbit squashes into a vertical ellipse; the top of the wave catches up with the bottom; when too steep the wave breaks.
- Swash: the rush of water up the shore after a wave breaks; it has a constructive effect, carrying material onto the shore.
- Backwash: the water flowing back towards the sea; it has a destructive effect, dragging material out to sea.

TYPES OF WAVES
- Constructive waves: swash more powerful than backwash, so more material is deposited than removed. Smaller in height, longer wavelength, break less often (fewer than 10 per minute). Produce a flatter, gently sloping beach. Also called spilling breakers.
- Destructive waves: backwash more powerful than swash, so more material is removed than built up. Higher, shorter wavelength, break more often (more than 10 per minute). Create a steeper beach profile. Also called plunging breakers.

WAVE REFRACTION
- Before material can be transported, natural processes turn intact cliff rock into small particles the waves can move.
- Wave refraction: waves bend and change direction as they approach the shore.
- Shallower water around a headland slows waves down; in deeper water at the sides, waves keep moving faster. This unequal movement makes the wave bend inwards around both sides of the headland.
- Wave energy converges (concentrates) on the headland, causing destructive erosion. By the time waves reach the bays they are less powerful and constructive, so they deposit (energy diverges).

PROCESSES OF COASTAL EROSION
- Coastal erosion is caused by destructive waves (backwash stronger than swash).
- Rate of coastal erosion depends on:
- Power of the wave: strong destructive waves erode more than weak constructive waves.
- Hardness of the rock: hard rock such as quartzite breaks down much more slowly than softer rock such as limestone.
- Slope of the beach: a higher beach profile is more open to wave attack than a gentle one.
- Shape of the coast: headlands and bays cause wave refraction, speeding up erosion at headlands and slowing it in bays.
- Rising sea levels: more sea water makes waves larger, more destructive and erosive.
- Human activity: removing sand for construction, farming and recreation lowers coastlines and speeds up erosion; defences such as rock armour and sea walls slow or prevent it.
- Hydraulic action: the force of waves crashing against the base of the coast, forcing water into cracks; over time cracks widen and material falls away.
- Compressed air (compression): the wave forces air into cracks a fraction of a second before the water arrives, trapping it. The air expands under pressure, widening cracks and shattering rock.
- Abrasion: loose eroded material (rocks, gravel, sand) carried by waves is hurled at the coast, widening and deepening cracks.
- Attrition: rocks and pebbles collide with each other as they are transported, becoming smaller, smoother and more rounded.
- Solution: weak carbonic acids in sea water dissolve soluble particles such as calcium carbonate in limestone and chalk.
- Example photo: cliff near Silver Strand, Barna, Co. Galway shows a notch formed by compressed air, freshly eroded rocks and rounded rocks (attrition).

COASTAL TRANSPORTATION: LONGSHORE DRIFT
- Longshore drift: the zig-zag movement of material sideways (laterally) along the coast.
- The prevailing wind makes waves approach the coast at an oblique angle, so the swash moves diagonally up the beach.
- The backwash flows straight back out to sea under gravity.
- Sand and silt are moved along the coast this way. Movement may be updrift or downdrift depending on currents and wind. Where the coastline bends, sediment keeps moving in a downdrift direction.

COASTAL DEPOSITION
- Deposition: when waves drop material (sand, rocks, pebbles) on the coast because they no longer have the energy to carry it.
- Carried out by constructive waves with stronger swash than backwash.
- Low-energy constructive waves form: in shallow waters such as bays where wave refraction slows waves; when waves enter sheltered areas such as bays or coves; in calm weather with little wind.
- Example: deposition is a prominent process in Dublin Bay (North Bull Island).

LANDFORMS OF COASTAL EROSION
- List: bays and headlands, sea caves, blowholes, sea arches, sea stacks and sea stumps, geos, sea cliffs and wave-cut platforms.

BAYS AND HEADLANDS
- Headland: a high piece of land that sticks out into the sea. Bay: a broad, inward-curving inlet of the sea.
- Examples of bays: Clew Bay, Co. Mayo; Dublin Bay. Headlands: Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo; Wicklow Head, Co. Wicklow.
- Processes: differential erosion, hydraulic action, compression, abrasion.
- Formation: they form where the coast has bands of hard rock (e.g. granite) and soft rock (e.g. limestone) next to each other. The soft rock is eroded much faster by hydraulic action, compression and abrasion. This is differential erosion. Waves attack joints and bedding planes, weakening them until they fall away.
- The soft rock wears back and the shoreline retreats inland to form a bay; the harder rock sticks out as a headland.
- Once the headland is prominent, wave refraction concentrates wave power on its sides, eroding it; in the bays waves are weaker and deposition is more likely.
- Diagram (Fig 11.12): original coastline, alternating hard and soft rock bands, headland of hard rock with stacks, bay of soft rock with deposition.

LANDFORMS ON A HEADLAND
- Sea cave, blowhole, sea arch, sea stack and sea stump, geo. Processes: differential erosion, wave refraction, hydraulic action, compression, abrasion, solution.
- Diagram (Fig 11.14): lines of weakness lead to a sea cave; a blowhole rises from the cave roof; an arch cuts through; collapse leaves a stack, then a stump.

SEA CAVES
- Tunnels or passages at a cliff face or headland. Example: Ballybunion, Co. Kerry. Processes: hydraulic action, compression, abrasion.
- Formed when softer, less resistant rock is eroded by hydraulic action and compression as destructive waves attack the side of a headland. A wave-cut notch forms; as it widens and deepens it becomes a cave, with abrasion playing a bigger role.

BLOWHOLES
- Chimney-like hollows linking the top of a headland to the roof of a sea cave. Example: Carrickabraghy Castle, Isle of Doagh, Co. Donegal. Process: compression.
- Air compressed in the cave expands upwards, weakening joints in the rock above. Over time a chimney breaks out on top. When water flows into the cave, air and seawater are pushed out through it, producing spray.

SEA ARCHES
- Bridge-shaped openings in a headland. Example: Great Pollet Sea Arch, Fanad, Co. Donegal. Processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, compression, solution.
- A cave breaks through to the other side of the headland; or two caves on either side join as wave refraction makes waves attack from both sides.

SEA STACKS AND SEA STUMPS
- Sea stack: a freestanding pillar of rock in the sea just off the coast. Example: Dun Briste, Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo. Processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, solution.
- The arch grows until the top can no longer be supported and collapses under gravity, leaving a stack.
- As the stack wears down it becomes a sea stump, then disappears under the sea. Example of a stump: Old Head of Kinsale, Co. Cork.

GEOS
- Tiny narrow inlets cut into the side of the coast. Example: Clare Island, Co. Mayo (near Strake). Processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, compression, solution.
- Form when the roof of a sea cave collapses or when waves exploit a narrow line of weakness; softer rock erodes faster than harder rock (differential erosion).

SEA CLIFFS AND WAVE-CUT PLATFORMS
- Cliff: a vertical slope where land and sea meet. Wave-cut platform (wave-cut terrace): a flat area of rock at the base of the cliff exposed at low tide.
- Examples: Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare; Sliabh Liag Cliffs, Co. Donegal. Geofact: Sliabh Liag, at 601 m, are the highest sea cliffs in Europe.
- Processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, compression, solution, undercutting.
- Destructive waves (more than ten per minute, stronger backwash) attack the coast by hydraulic action, especially in gales and storms.
- Abrasion hurls stones at the coast between high and low water marks. Weaknesses are exposed and a wave-cut notch forms (a small gash cut into the coast).
- Swash pushes into the notch compressing air in cracks; when the backwash retreats the pressure is released explosively.
- The notch grows; the unsupported overhang becomes unstable (undercutting) and collapses, forming a vertical cliff face. Solution dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone.
- Repeated over and over, the cliff retreats inland leaving a wave-cut platform of more resistant rock, visible at low tide and smoothed by attrition.
- The platform protects the cliff by absorbing incoming wave energy.
- Above the high tide mark, the cliff is weakened by weathering (freeze-thaw) and mass movement such as rotational slumping (sections slide down in a curved way).
- In time the cliff becomes inactive once it has retreated out of reach of the sea.

LANDFORMS OF COASTAL DEPOSITION
- Caused by constructive waves (swash stronger than backwash). Landforms: beach, sand spit, sand bar, tombolo, lagoon.
- Geofact: the longest beach in Ireland is Fermoyle Strand, Dingle Peninsula, Co. Kerry, about 11.5 km, part of Brandon Bay.
- Geofact: the world's longest continuous sandy beach is Praia do Cassino, Brazil, 254 km; the sand is so hard it is used as a highway; dunes separate it from Lagoa dos Patos, a lagoon of 10,100 km2.

BEACH
- A gently sloping area of loose deposited material (sand or shingle) between high and low tide marks. Shingle: loose pebbles and gravel.
- Examples: Carrownisky Beach, Louisburgh, Co. Mayo; Fermoyle Strand, Co. Kerry.
- Processes: low-energy constructive waves, wave refraction, longshore drift.
- Wave refraction concentrates power on headlands; waves reach bays with less energy.
- In sheltered bays and calm conditions, a powerful swash carries material up the shore; the weak backwash cannot carry it back, so more is deposited than removed.
- Sorting: strong swash and weak backwash sort material; heavier stone and shingle is left at the backshore, lighter fine sand is carried to the foreshore, giving a gently graded profile.
- Longshore drift spreads the beach sideways; most material is deposited from the direction of the prevailing wind.
- Beaches range from long straight beaches to small curved pocket beaches in small sheltered bays.

BEACH PROFILE
- Three sections: foreshore, middle shore, backshore. Smaller, steeper beaches have only foreshore and backshore (storm beach).
- Foreshore: very fine sand, often wet. Ridges form parallel to the coast where constructive waves break. Runnels: water-filled depressions between ridges.
- Middle shore: slightly coarser sand, often dry. Ripples: gentle lines in sand made by swash. Cusps: temporary semi-circular depressions of coarser sand and gravel, in a regular row, same size. Berms: small ridges of shingle and stones deposited by low-energy waves as the tide comes in.
- Backshore (storm beach): storm waves throw stones and pebbles above normal high tide. Wind carries sand from the foreshore until it meets an obstacle (fence, rock, vegetation), building sand dunes. Dunes are not stable; councils plant marram grass to hold them.

SAND SPIT, SAND BAR, TOMBOLO AND LAGOON
- Sand spit: a ridge of deposits (sand, shingle) extending out into the sea from the coast. Examples: Portmarnock, Co. Dublin; Glenbeigh, Co. Kerry.
- Spits form where the coastline changes direction and in shallow, sheltered water. Longshore drift moves sand, silt and pebbles along in a zig-zag. Constructive waves deposit more than they remove. Heavier material is deposited near the mainland, finer material at the far end. The end may curve due to wind and currents. Marram grass stabilises it; the sheltered water behind can become a salt marsh.
- Sand bar: a long ridge of deposits in the sea. Baymouth bar: joins two headlands, cutting off a bay, when a spit grows across the bay mouth. Water trapped behind forms a lagoon (salt lake). Example: Rusheen Bay, Barna, Co. Galway (sandbar and lagoon).
- Offshore bar: not connected to the mainland; forms when underwater currents move against surface currents, making waves break early and deposit material.
- Tombolo: a ridge of deposits joining an island to the mainland, formed by constructive waves and longshore drift; the sheltered area between island and mainland encourages deposition. Examples: Howth Head, Co. Dublin; Omey Island, Co. Galway.

APPLIED GEOGRAPHY PROJECT (FIELDWORK IDEAS)
- Research the coast on maps and photos; observe landforms; orientation with map and compass; measure beach, dune and platform; measure slope angles and cliff height; wave count; wave height; rate and direction of longshore drift; sketch profiles; analyse material size, shape and rock type; note human interference; write a report.

COASTAL MANAGEMENT AND PROTECTION STRATEGY
- The Inter-Departmental Group on National Coastal Change Management Strategy identified five approaches:
- 1. Do nothing: no intervention; land is lost to the sea over time.
- 2. Hold the line: build or maintain defences to protect the coastline.
- 3. Managed realignment: move defences or the coastline landward to a new, more sustainable line.
- 4. Managed retreat: coordinate moving people and infrastructure away from risk and let the coast retreat.
- 5. Advance the line: build defences out at sea, e.g. tidal barrage, land reclamation.

CASE STUDY: HARD ENGINEERING AT SALTHILL, CO. GALWAY
- Salthill is on Galway Bay just west of Galway City; a major tourist attraction since the 19th century; thousands 'walk the Prom', use the beach or go sea swimming. Galway City Council invested heavily in hard engineering.
- Rock armour: gradual slope that reduces the erosive power of water, stopping hydraulic action and abrasion; main job is to reduce wave energy; often placed at an angle in front of old, too-vertical sea walls.
- Recurved (wave return) sea wall: turns the breaking wave back on itself in storm surges. The curve and lip fling the swash back out to sea, so the backwash cannot erode the beach in front.
- Steps on some sea walls absorb wave energy and make waves break. One-way storm drain holes let floodwater flow back out but not in.
- Groynes: long lines of boulders or low wooden/concrete walls at right angles to the shore; trap sediment and stop longshore drift removing the beach (boulder groynes at Salthill).
- Sustainability: very effective; unlikely waves pass a well-designed sea wall. But damages landscape and habitat, unsightly and very expensive: 1 m of sea wall costs more than 1 m of motorway. Economically unsustainable except for a few large towns like Galway where seaside tourism matters.
- Groynes keep beaches in place but starve areas downshore of deposition, increasing erosion there.
- Best to manage natural protection (beaches, wetlands, sand dunes) to avoid hard engineering.

CASE STUDY: SOFT ENGINEERING AT ENNISCRONE BEACH, CO. SLIGO
- 2023: 'Protect Our Dunes' initiative to protect the Enniscrone dunes, about 5 km long, one of the longest in Ireland. Aim: raise awareness; ask people to stay off dunes, keep to pathways and camping areas, follow signs, watch wildlife from a distance.
- Low-lying areas depend on beaches and dunes for natural flood defence. Beaches absorb wave energy; dunes are built from sand blown up from the beach above high tide.
- Marram grass traps sand and slows the wind so sand is deposited; it is very hardy, can survive being buried by a metre of sand each year and quickly recolonises storm-damaged dunes.
- Threats: trampling kills vegetation; paths through dunes act as wind tunnels blowing sand inland; cars and horses compact sand so less loose sand blows onto the dunes.
- Solutions: reroute footpaths; keep cars and horses off the beach; wooden boardwalks to prevent trampling and deep hollows; porous fencing traps sand so dunes build up behind it. Cheap: porous fencing costs EUR 5 to 25 per metre.
- Sustainability: very effective, no damage to landscape or habitat, no unsightly concrete, environmentally friendly, less intrusive, low-cost and easy to maintain compared with hard engineering.

SUMMARY
- Waves get their power from the wind. Constructive waves deposit; destructive waves erode.
- Five erosion processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, compression, attrition, solution. Transport sideways by longshore drift. Deposition in calm, sheltered bays.
- Hard and soft engineering both work, but soft methods are more environmentally and economically sustainable.

EXAM SKILLS
- SEC HL Sample Paper Q3(a): examine how transportation and deposition formed one named coastal landform, with labelled diagram. Best choice: a beach (e.g. Carrownisky), covering constructive waves, wave refraction, swash/backwash, sorting, longshore drift and the beach profile features. It must be an Irish example.

rows.prompt: What is meant by the fetch of a wave?
options: The distance of ocean over which the wind blows
The height between the crest and the trough
The speed at which a wave breaks on shore
The number of waves breaking each minute
rows.explanation: Fetch is the distance of ocean over which the wind blows and waves build up. A bigger fetch gives bigger, more powerful waves.

rows.prompt: What is the top of a wave called?
rows.explanation: The crest is the top of the wave, which is pulled up; the trough is the dip, which is pushed down.

rows.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three things that decide the size and energy of a wave?
options: Length of time the wind blows
rows.explanation: Wave size depends on wind strength, how long the wind blows and the fetch. Rock hardness affects the rate of erosion, not wave size.

rows.prompt: Why are Lahinch and Easkey good places for surfing?
options: They have very calm sheltered bays
They face the Irish Sea with strong tides
They have a huge fetch across the Atlantic
They have many offshore sand bars
rows.explanation: The west coast has a fetch of thousands of kilometres across the Atlantic, so large waves build up.

rows.prompt: What happens to waves as they move from deep water into shallow water?
options: They slow down and become steeper
They speed up and become flatter
rows.explanation: Friction with the seabed slows waves down; they get steeper, closer together, and their orbit becomes an ellipse until they break.

rows.prompt: What is the backwash?
options: Water rushing up the beach after a wave breaks
Water flowing back towards the sea
Wind blowing sand up onto the dunes
Air trapped in cracks in a cliff
rows.explanation: Backwash is the water flowing back to the sea after the swash. It drags material out to sea.

rows.prompt: Constructive waves usually break how often?
rows.explanation: Constructive waves break less often, fewer than 10 per minute; destructive waves break more than 10 per minute.

rows.prompt: Which describes a destructive wave?
options: Strong swash, weak backwash, gentle beach
Weak swash, strong backwash, steep beach
rows.explanation: Destructive waves have a stronger backwash than swash, are higher with shorter wavelength and create a steep beach profile.

rows.prompt: Destructive waves are sometimes called what?
rows.explanation: Destructive waves are called plunging breakers; constructive waves are called spilling breakers.

rows.prompt: In wave refraction, where is wave energy concentrated?
rows.explanation: Waves bend around headlands, so their energy converges there and causes erosion; in the bays the energy spreads out and deposition happens.

rows.prompt: Which erosion process is the force of waves crashing against the coast and forcing water into cracks?
rows.explanation: Hydraulic action is the sheer force of the waves pushing water into cracks, which widen until material falls away.

rows.prompt: Which process makes rocks and pebbles smaller, smoother and rounder as they hit each other?
rows.explanation: Attrition is when transported rocks collide with each other and become smaller, smoother and more rounded.

rows.prompt: Solution mainly attacks which rocks on the coast?
rows.explanation: Weak carbonic acids in sea water dissolve calcium carbonate, found in limestone and chalk.

rows.prompt: How does compressed air break down cliffs?
options: Air dissolves the minerals in the rock
Trapped air expands under pressure and widens cracks
Air carries sand that scrapes the cliff
Air cools the rock until it splits
rows.explanation: Air is trapped in cracks just before the water arrives; it expands under pressure, widening the cracks and shattering the rock.

rows.prompt: Why does quartzite erode more slowly than limestone?
options: It is harder and more resistant
It is found only in bays
It is always below sea level
rows.explanation: The hardness of the rock affects the rate of erosion; hard, resistant quartzite takes much longer to break down than softer limestone.

rows.prompt: In longshore drift, how does the backwash move?
options: Straight back out to sea under gravity
rows.explanation: The swash moves diagonally up the beach at an oblique angle, but the backwash flows straight back to sea under gravity, giving a zig-zag movement.

rows.prompt: In which situation are waves most likely to deposit material?
options: In stormy weather with strong gales
In calm weather in a sheltered bay
When waves have a long fetch
At the tip of a headland
rows.explanation: Low-energy constructive waves deposit material in shallow, sheltered bays and coves and in calm weather.

rows.prompt: Bays and headlands form by which process when hard and soft rock lie side by side?
rows.explanation: Differential erosion wears soft rock (e.g. limestone) back into bays faster than hard rock (e.g. granite), which is left as headlands.

rows.prompt: Which of these is an example of a headland given in the chapter?
rows.explanation: Downpatrick Head and Wicklow Head are the headland examples; Clew Bay is a bay.

rows.prompt: Where is the blowhole example used in the chapter?
options: Old Head of Kinsale, Co. Cork
rows.explanation: The blowhole example is at Carrickabraghy Castle, Isle of Doagh, Co. Donegal; Ballybunion is the sea cave example.

rows.prompt: What forms when a sea arch collapses under gravity?
rows.explanation: When the top of the arch can no longer be supported, it collapses and leaves a freestanding pillar called a sea stack, e.g. Dun Briste.

rows.prompt: What is a geo?
options: A pillar of rock off the coast
A ridge joining an island to land
A tiny narrow inlet in the coast
A salt lake behind a sand bar
rows.explanation: A geo is a tiny narrow inlet formed when a cave roof collapses or waves exploit a line of weakness, e.g. on Clare Island.

rows.prompt: Which are the highest sea cliffs in Europe?
rows.explanation: Sliabh Liag Cliffs in Co. Donegal reach 601 m above sea level, the highest sea cliffs in Europe.

rows.prompt: How does a wave-cut platform protect a cliff?
options: It traps sand to build dunes
It turns waves back on themselves
It absorbs the energy of incoming waves
rows.explanation: The flat wave-cut platform absorbs wave energy, so less reaches the cliff, and eventually the cliff becomes inactive.

rows.prompt: On a beach, where does the heavier material (stones and shingle) end up after sorting?
rows.explanation: Strong swash and weak backwash leave heavy stone and shingle at the backshore, while fine sand is carried to the foreshore.

rows.prompt: What are cusps?
options: Small ridges of shingle left at high tide
Semi-circular depressions in a regular row
Gentle lines in the sand made by swash
rows.explanation: Cusps are temporary semi-circular depressions of coarser sand and gravel, in a row, the same size and regularly spaced.

rows.prompt: A ridge of deposits that joins an island to the mainland is a...
rows.explanation: A tombolo joins an island to the mainland, e.g. Omey Island, Co. Galway and Howth Head, Co. Dublin.

rows.prompt: A lagoon forms when...
options: a baymouth bar traps water behind it
a groyne traps sand on a beach
rock armour is placed in a bay
rows.explanation: When a spit grows across a bay mouth to form a baymouth bar, the trapped water becomes a salt lake called a lagoon.

rows.prompt: Which coastal management approach coordinates moving people and infrastructure away from risk?
rows.explanation: Managed retreat moves people and infrastructure away from the risk and allows the coastline to retreat.

rows.prompt: What is the main purpose of groynes?
options: To turn breaking waves back out to sea
To trap sediment and stop longshore drift
To let floodwater drain back to the sea
rows.explanation: Groynes are built at right angles to the shore to trap sediment and stop longshore drift carrying the beach away.

rows.prompt: Which fact shows hard engineering is very expensive?
options: Porous fencing costs up to 25 euro per metre
Marram grass survives a metre of sand
Sea walls have one-way storm drains
A metre of sea wall costs more than a metre of motorway
rows.explanation: It is estimated 1 m of sea wall costs more to build than 1 m of motorway, making it economically unsustainable for most places.

rows.prompt: Why does trampling damage sand dunes?
options: It kills the vegetation holding the sand
It adds too much sand to the dunes
It increases the fetch of waves
rows.explanation: Constant trampling kills vegetation such as marram grass, leaving the dunes vulnerable to wind and storms.

rows.prompt: Explain two differences between constructive and destructive waves.
rows.model_answer: Constructive waves have a stronger swash than backwash, so they deposit material and build a gently sloping beach; destructive waves have a stronger backwash, so they remove material and make a steeper beach. Constructive waves are lower with a longer wavelength and break fewer than 10 times a minute, while destructive waves are higher with a shorter wavelength and break more than 10 times a minute.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words how wave refraction works.
rows.model_answer: Waves bend as they approach the shore. Near a headland the water is shallow, so the waves slow down, but in the deeper water at the sides they keep moving faster. This makes the waves bend around both sides of the headland, concentrating their power on it and eroding it, while the waves reaching the bays are weaker and deposit material.

rows.prompt: Name and briefly explain the processes of coastal erosion.
rows.model_answer: Hydraulic action is the force of waves pushing water into cracks. Compressed air is air trapped in cracks that expands and shatters rock. Abrasion is waves throwing rocks and sand at the coast. Attrition is rocks hitting each other and becoming smaller and rounder, and solution is carbonic acid in sea water dissolving calcium carbonate in limestone and chalk.

rows.prompt: Describe three factors that influence the rate of coastal erosion.
rows.model_answer: The power of the wave matters, as strong destructive waves erode more than weak constructive ones. The hardness of the rock matters, as hard quartzite erodes much more slowly than soft limestone. Rising sea levels make waves larger and more erosive, and human activity such as removing sand speeds erosion up while sea walls and rock armour slow it down.

rows.prompt: Draw and label a diagram of longshore drift (describe it in words), and explain the process.
rows.model_answer: The diagram shows the sea, a beach, the prevailing wind direction and arrows showing the swash going diagonally up the beach and the backwash coming straight down, making a zig-zag path, with an arrow for the overall movement of sand along the coast. The prevailing wind makes waves hit the coast at an oblique angle, so the swash carries sand diagonally up the beach, and gravity pulls the backwash straight back, moving sand and silt sideways along the coast.

rows.prompt: Briefly describe how a blowhole is formed, naming an Irish example.
rows.model_answer: A blowhole forms when air is compressed inside a sea cave and expands upwards, weakening joints in the rock above. Over time a chimney-like hollow breaks through to the top of the headland. When water rushes into the cave, air and seawater are forced out through it as spray. An example is at Carrickabraghy Castle, Isle of Doagh, Co. Donegal.

rows.prompt: Name the three sections of a beach profile and one feature found in each.
rows.model_answer: The foreshore has very fine wet sand with ridges and water-filled runnels between them. The middle shore has slightly coarser sand with ripples, cusps and berms. The backshore, or storm beach, has stones and pebbles thrown up by storm waves, with sand dunes behind.

rows.prompt: What is 'managed retreat'? Name two other approaches to coastal management.
rows.model_answer: Managed retreat means coordinating the movement of people and infrastructure away from coastal risks and allowing the coastline to retreat. Other approaches are 'do nothing', where natural processes take over, and 'hold the line', where coastal defences are built or maintained. Managed realignment and advance the line are also approaches.

rows.prompt: In relation to one named coastal landform that you studied, examine how the processes of transportation and deposition led to its formation. Use a labelled diagram to illustrate your answer. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Named landform: a beach, e.g. Carrownisky Beach, Louisburgh, Co. Mayo. A beach is a gently sloping area of sand or shingle between the high and low tide marks. Beaches are formed by constructive waves. Wave refraction concentrates wave power on the headlands, so waves reach the bay with less energy. In sheltered bays and calm conditions the waves break with a powerful swash that carries material up the shore. The backwash is weak, so more material is deposited than is taken away. This sorts the material: heavy stones and shingle stay at the backshore while fine sand is carried to the foreshore, giving a gently graded profile. Longshore drift transports material sideways in a zig-zag, as waves approach at an oblique angle with the prevailing wind and the backwash returns straight under gravity, spreading the beach out. The foreshore has fine sand, ridges and runnels. The middle shore has coarser sand, ripples, cusps and berms. Storm waves throw pebbles above high tide to form the storm beach, and wind-blown sand trapped by obstacles forms sand dunes, held in place by marram grass. Diagram: beach profile showing low and high tide marks, foreshore with ridges and runnels, middle shore with cusps and berms, backshore storm beach and dunes with marram grass.

Maximum 30m; Irish example required.

rows.prompt: Examine the formation of one landform of coastal erosion that you have studied, with the aid of a labelled diagram. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Named landform: a sea cliff and wave-cut platform, e.g. Sliabh Liag Cliffs, Co. Donegal, the highest sea cliffs in Europe at 601 m. A cliff is a vertical slope where land meets sea. Destructive waves, with a stronger backwash than swash and breaking more than ten times a minute, attack the coast by hydraulic action, especially in gales. Through abrasion they hurl stones at the coast between the high and low water marks, exposing weaknesses and cutting a wave-cut notch. As the swash pushes into the notch, air is compressed in cracks; when the backwash retreats the pressure is released explosively, widening them. Solution dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone. The notch grows and the overhang is undercut until it collapses, leaving a vertical cliff face. This repeats and the cliff retreats inland, leaving a wave-cut platform of resistant rock visible at low tide, smoothed by attrition. The platform absorbs wave energy and protects the cliff. Above high tide the cliff is weakened by freeze-thaw and rotational slumping. Eventually the cliff becomes inactive when it is out of reach of the sea. Diagram: cliff with original position, wave-cut notch, overhang, direction of cliff retreat and wave-cut platform.

Examination: 11 SRPs x 2m = 22m (e.g. destructive waves; over 10 per minute; hydraulic action; abrasion between tide marks; wave-cut notch; compressed air; solution of limestone; undercutting; collapse of overhang; cliff retreat; wave-cut platform at low tide; attrition smooths platform; platform absorbs energy; freeze-thaw/slumping; inactive cliff). Maximum 30m.

rows.prompt: Describe one hard engineering method of coastal protection that you have studied and analyse its effectiveness. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: At Salthill, Co. Galway, a major tourist attraction where thousands walk the Prom, Galway City Council has invested heavily in hard engineering. A recurved, or wave return, sea wall turns breaking waves back on themselves in storm surges: the curve and lip fling the swash back out, so the backwash cannot erode the beach in front. Steps absorb wave energy and one-way storm drains let floodwater flow back to sea. Rock armour, with a gradual slope, reduces wave energy and stops hydraulic action and abrasion, and boulder groynes trap sediment against longshore drift. These defences are very effective; even big winter storms rarely get past a well-designed sea wall. However, they damage the natural landscape and habitat, are unsightly and very expensive, as 1 m of sea wall costs more than 1 m of motorway. Groynes also starve beaches downshore of sand, increasing erosion there. So hard engineering is only economically sustainable in large towns like Galway where tourism is important.
rows.marking_scheme: Named method and location 2m. Description: 4 SRPs x 2m = 8m (e.g. recurved wall turns waves back; protects beach from backwash; steps absorb energy; storm drains; rock armour reduces wave energy; groynes trap sediment). Analysis of effectiveness: 5 SRPs x 2m = 10m (e.g. very effective in storms; damages landscape/habitat; unsightly; very expensive - sea wall vs motorway; groynes increase erosion downshore; only sustainable for large tourist towns). Maximum 20m.

rows.prompt: Discuss how sand dunes can be managed as a soft engineering method of coastal protection, with reference to an Irish example. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: At Enniscrone Beach, Co. Sligo, whose 5 km dune system is one of the longest in Ireland, the 'Protect Our Dunes' initiative began in 2023. It asks people to stay off the dunes, use designated pathways and camping areas, follow signs and watch wildlife from a distance. Healthy dunes protect low-lying land from flooding because they are built from sand blown up from the beach above high tide. Marram grass traps the sand and slows the wind; it survives being buried by a metre of sand a year and quickly recolonises storm damage. Trampling kills this vegetation, paths through dunes act as wind tunnels blowing sand inland, and cars and horses compact the sand so less blows onto the dunes. Solutions include rerouting footpaths, banning cars and horses, building wooden boardwalks and erecting porous fencing to trap sand, which costs only EUR 5 to 25 per metre. These methods are effective, cheap, easy to maintain and do not damage the landscape, so they are more sustainable than hard engineering.
rows.marking_scheme: Named example 2m. Maximum 20m.
